newsitem.title: USA: FAA rejects ValuJet's planned expansion.
newsitem.headline: FAA rejects ValuJet's planned expansion.

text.p: The Federal Aviation Administration Wednesday denied ValuJet airlines permission to resume service between Atlanta and Dallas/Forth Worth, West Palm Beach or Fort Myers.
Valujet was allowed to resume a limited schedule in late September after being grounded in the wake of a May 11 crash in the Florida Everglades that killed all 110 people on board.
Under an agreement with the FAA, the low-cost carrier is required to obtain authority from the agency to expand beyond its current fleet of 15 aircraft.

"ValuJet has recently sought permission ... to expand its operating fleet to West Palm Beach and Fort Myers in Florida, and Dallas/Forth Worth in Texas, but the agency has not at this time permitted the expansion," the FAA said in a written statement.
The FAA gave no reason for denying the request, but noted that its decision meant ValuJet would be unable to serve customers who had already purchased tickets for these routes.

The agency said it was considering ValuJet's request to arrange charter services with other airlines beginning Thursday and continuing through Jan. 6. It advised the company to stop selling tickets for any new service after that date.

"Currently the Department of Transportation is reviewing ValuJet's charter arrangements to ensure full compliance with FAA safety standards," the statement said. Approval of charters would be granted only when the FAA was completely satisfied, it added.

ValuJet had sold 15,000 tickets for flights between Dec. 19 and Jan. 6 on routes that it had not received approval to operate, the FAA said. It advised passengers holding tickets to the Florida or Texas destinations to contact the airline.

The Atlanta-based carrier was grounded in June after Flight 592 plunged into the Everglades. Following a series of internal reforms, ValuJet resumed operations under close FAA scrutiny on Sept. 30, but with only a fraction of the service it provided before the crash.

The cause of the accident has not yet been formally determined by the National Transportation Safety Board, but investigators think that oxygen generators loaded into the plane's cargo hold by a subcontractor may have ignited, triggering a fire.
